questions.stem:
Solve the literal equation for \(x\):
\(\frac{px + q}{b} = c\)
questions.hint: Rearrange the equation to isolate x on one side.
questions.solution:
Solving the literal equation:
\(\frac{px + q}{b} = c\)
1. Multiply by b: px + q = bc
2. Subtract q: px = bc - q
3. Divide by p: x = \frac{bc-q}{p}

steps.explain: Multiply both sides by \\(b\\) to clear the denominator.
steps.work: \\(\\frac{px + q}{b} \\times b = c \\times b \\implies px + q = bc\\)
\\(px + q - q = bc - q \\implies px = bc - q\\)

steps.explain: Divide both sides by \\(p\\) to isolate \\(x\\).

questions.stem: When a mathematics teacher was asked her age she replied, 'One-fourth of my age five years ago, when added to half my age last year, gives my age nine years ago.' How old is she?
questions.hint: Let her age be x, and construct the equation using the fractions of (x - 5) and (x - 1).
questions.solution:
Let the teacher's age be \(x\).
Age five years ago = \(x - 5\).
Age last year = \(x - 1\).
Age nine years ago = \(x - 9\).
Equation:
\[\frac{x - 5}{4} +  rac{x - 1}{2} = x - 9\]
Multiply both sides by 4:
\[(x - 5) + 2(x - 1) = 4(x - 9)\]
\[x - 5 + 2x - 2 = 4x - 36\]
\[3x - 7 = 4x - 36 \Rightarrow x = 29\]
So she is \(29\) years old.

questions.stem: A river flows at \(4\text{ km/h}\). A boat goes upstream \(\frac{3}{5}\) as fast as downstream. What is the speed of the boat in still water in \(\text{km/h}\)?
questions.hint: Set Upstream speed = (3/5) * Downstream speed.
questions.solution:
Let the speed of the boat in still water be \(v\text{ km/h}\).
Upstream speed = \(v - 4\).
Downstream speed = \(v + 4\).
Upstream speed is \(\frac{3}{5}\) of downstream speed:
\[v - 4 = \frac{3}{5}(v + 4)\]
\[5(v - 4) = 3(v + 4)\]
\[5v - 20 = 3v + 12\]
\[2v = 32 \Rightarrow v = 16\text{ km/h}\]
So the speed in still water is \(16\text{ km/h}\).

So Vat A has \(5\%\) butter-fat.

questions.stem: A salesman makes a trip to visit a client. The traffic keeps his average speed to \(60\text{ km/h}\). On the return trip, he takes a route \(10\text{ km}\) longer, but he averages \(80\text{ km/h}\). If he takes the same time each way, how long was the total journey in \(\text{km}\)?
questions.hint: Set up outward time = return time. Find the outward distance first, then calculate the total distance.
questions.solution:
Let the outward distance be \(d\text{ km}\). Then the return distance is \(d + 10\text{ km}\).
Time = Distance / Speed.
Outward time = \(\frac{d}{60}\).
Return time = \(\frac{d + 10}{80}\).
Since the times are equal:
\[\frac{d}{60} = \frac{d + 10}{80}\]
\[80d = 60(d + 10)\]
\[80d = 60d + 600\]
\[20d = 600 \Rightarrow d = 30\text{ km}\]
Outward distance = \(30\text{ km}\), Return distance = \(30 + 10 = 40\text{ km}\).
Total distance = \(30 + 40 = 70\text{ km}\).

questions.stem: A person has twice as many 20-cent coins as 10-cent coins. If their total value is \(\$25\), how many 10-cent coins are there?
questions.hint: Let the number of 10-cent coins be \(x\). Then 20-cent coins = \(2x\). Write the total value in cents.
questions.solution:
Let the number of 10-cent coins be \(x\). Then the number of 20-cent coins is \(2x\).

Total value = \(10(x) + 20(2x) = 2500\) cents.

\(10x + 40x = 2500 \Rightarrow 50x = 2500 \Rightarrow x = 50\).

So there are 50 of the 10-cent coins.
